Newly emerged prolarvae of Yellowtail trumpeter have an initial wet weight of just 0.000092 grams [Wwb = 0.000092 grams], a minuscule starting mass typical for a pelagic teleost larva that must quickly undergo yolk-sac resorption and transition to exogenous feeding. Following a period of rapid larval growth and the commencement of juvenile recruitment, individuals begin to approach their ultimate total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], a size that represents the asymptotic body length observed in older, fully grown fish from estuarine populations. The length-weight relationship derived from field specimens indicates that at this ultimate size, the corresponding maximum recorded body mass in adults reaches 399 grams [Wwi = 399 grams], confirming a robust, moderately deep-bodied morphology well-suited to the species' demersal foraging habits in coastal seagrass beds.

Puberty in Yellowtail trumpeter is attained relatively early in the life cycle, marking the transition from a growing juvenile to a sexually mature adult capable of gametogenesis. The total length at puberty is approximately 12 centimeters [Lp = approximately 12 centimeters], a size typically reached by the end of the first year or early in the second year of life depending on local productivity regimes. At this length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 25 grams [Wwp = approximately 25 grams], a body mass that reflects a threshold of somatic development sufficient to support the energetic demands of gonad maturation and the onset of vitellogenesis in females. Field surveys of age-structured populations confirm that individuals attaining this size become reproductively active during the subsequent spawning season, contributing to the species' iteroparous reproductive strategy within subtropical Australian estuaries.

Mature individuals of Amniataba caudavittata show a predictable pattern of reproductive output linked to their body size. During a typical spawning event, gravid females produce a clutch of between 10,000 and 15,000 fertilised ova [N_R_i = a clutch of between 10,000 and 15,000 fertilised ova], each less than a millimeter in diameter, which are broadcast into the water column for external fertilisation. The frequency of these spawning events is modulated by seasonal thermal regimes, with most adults participating in one to two clutches per year [F_R_i = one to two clutches per year] over the protracted breeding period extending from spring through early autumn. This combination of high fecundity per event and moderate spawning frequency is characteristic of many tropical and subtropical terapontids, compensating for the high mortality rates suffered by pelagic eggs and early-stage larvae.

The maximum lifespan of Yellowtail trumpeter, documented under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], reaches nine years [am = nine years] — a notably extended duration for a terapontid of its moderate adult body size. While many related species in similar thermal environments typically exhibit maximum ages of five to seven years, this longevity likely reflects a combination of stable thermal conditions, low natural predation rates within seagrass habitats, and a metabolic regime that does not impose accelerated senescence. In wild populations exposed to fluctuating temperatures and variable food availability, maximum ages may be somewhat lower, though mark-recapture studies have confirmed the presence of eight-year-old individuals in protected estuarine reserves, further underscoring the species' capacity for extended survival under favorable conditions.

Growth trajectories following the larval-juvenile transition are characterised by an initial phase of rapid mass gain, with the wet weight at puberty of approximately 25 grams [Wwp = approximately 25 grams] attained within twelve to eighteen months of hatching under favourable conditions. Subsequent growth decelerates as fish approach the asymptotic adult body mass of 399 grams [Wwi = 399 grams], a pattern consistent with a von Bertalanffy-type growth curve common among iteroparous estuarine fishes. The total length at puberty of approximately 12 centimeters [Lp = approximately 12 centimeters] represents about forty percent of the ultimate total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], a proportional size at maturation that aligns closely with life-history predictions for species experiencing moderate to high adult survival rates. This allocation strategy prioritises early reproduction while still allowing sufficient somatic growth to reach a large terminal size.
